418.t: Blanche Calloway's records and Line of Jive
418.s: Morgenstern has a Calloway record he thinks has Dickenson on a Swedish LP; Dickenson has never heard it and asks for a cassette.
418.q: I've never heard it. I wish you'd make me a cassette of it.

418.t: Blanche Calloway's records and Line of Jive
418.s: Morgenstern has a Calloway record he thinks has Dickenson on it; Dickenson has never heard it and asks for a cassette.
418.ch: Early bands, Calloway to Basie and Kansas City (third typescript)
418.q: Yeah. But I never did hear any of them -- the ones I made. I --

418.t: Blanche Calloway's records and Line of Jive
418.s: Morgenstern has a Calloway record he thinks has Dickenson; Dickenson has never heard it and asks for a cassette.
418.q: Yeah. But I never did hear any of them -- the ones I made. I --

251.t: Wabash Blues and the Troy Floyd recordings
251.s: Albert doubts Troy made Wabash Blues but has a copy and thinks he and Charlie Dixon played on it; the recordings took three or four days.
251.q: Now, that's a little controversial there. Yeah. As far as I know, Troy did not make this Wabash Blues, but I have a copy of it at my home in San Antonio. I can't recall who the musicians on there just by playing it, but it seems to me that I can remember that I was part of that Wabash Blues, I'm…

251.t: Ben Norrisingle's records and Troy Floyd band members
251.s: Discussion of Hattie Burleson and Ben Norrisingle records, accompanied by a group out of Troy Floyd's band; Charlie Dixon has the recordings.
251.ch: Records and the Don Albert band
251.q: That's right. That part is right. Because one of them still lives here in San Antonio is the old man now, Charlie Dixon. He has all of those recordings.

857.t: Spanish Fort job and the Original Tuxedo Rag
857.s: They ask about the Spanish Fort engagement and where the records were made, then listen to Original Tuxedo Rag and talk of the rhythm section playing together.
857.q: He played before? Before. We went to Apple. You recorded in the fort? Huh? Where were you recording? No, we was playing at the Spanish Fort.

857.t: Unreleased takes and the number of Celestin records
857.s: They discuss unreleased tunes such as Alamazoo, the recording man, and the four early full-band records versus three later ones.
857.q: Yeah, he was very nice. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, because the last records we made, we made four records. And I haven't heard but three of them. Yeah. The last records we made, we made four. I've only heard of three.

877.t: Early unissued records and Gilbert Young
877.s: Handy recalls making records on Rampart Street that were never issued, and playing with Gilbert Young.
877.q: I can't just recall. But anyway, I played with Gilbert. Gilbert Young. You know Gilbert Young? I played with Gilbert Young. I imagine... I couldn't tell you exactly how many I have right off the reel, you know? But after you leave, I imagine it's different people I could recall that I can't just…

877.t: Recordings with Joe Robichaux and the Rhapsodians
877.s: Handy remembers recording with Joe Robichaux on Dumaine and North Rampart (J&M) and at WWL with the Rhapsodians; he is unsure whether anything came out.
877.q: I did. That's right. That's what I say. After you would... After you leave, I could recall and I have made a record with Joe Robichaux. And Joe Robichaux and I, we've been all in Texas, County, Texas. And we had some nice engagements up there.

602.t: Recordings with McShann, Bucktown Boogie, Roy Brown sides
602.s: Gabriel lists records made with McShann, Witherspoon and others, his feature Bucktown Boogie, and about twenty sides with Roy Brown and with Danny Barker.
602.q: I recorded with Mercury. And, oh, I can, with Jimmy Witherspoon singing. Charles Waterford singing. We did a lot of recording in St. Louis. We did some recording in California. Mm-hmm. Now, I don't keep them. Only a couple of the numbers. One I can remember because I named the number and it was my…

602.t: Danny Barker sessions: Joe Parrish, Mop Mop Brown, sidemen
602.s: Questions about the pianist on Danny and Lou Barker dates lead to Joe Parrish, Willow Weep for Me, Mop Mop Brown and its sidemen.
602.q: Joe Parrish. They called him Joe Parrish. We called him Joe Parrish. He's in Chicago now. Yeah. He's a terrific pianist, terrific vibe man too. Yeah. I just talked with him three weeks ago. I was coming from Minnesota and I stopped in Chicago.

833.t: The Shields family and the Third Street recording musicians
833.s: Robinson places the Shields on Third Street, hears the neighbours practise, and Russell mentions the New Orleans Owls.
833.ch: Early New Orleans recording bands and Third Street
833.q: Back there, they were living back there. But the Shields did live on 3rd street. 3rd street. 3rd street is right. That's where they lived. Mm-hmm. On 3rd street.

833.t: Trying to name musicians on Third Street who made records
833.s: He cannot recall the names of white musicians who lived near him and made records; Russell suggests Shields, Byersdorfer and others.
833.ch: Early New Orleans recording bands and Third Street
833.q: Oh, I used to, oh, John, I can't call them boys' names. Yeah, they used to make records there. I know one fellow that... Let me see if he can call his name.

1010.t: West End Roof Garden days and the Columbia recording contract
1010.s: All-night party jobs, rehearsals with Newcomb girls, then Columbia asks for an original number and the band later records 15 sides in Atlanta.
1010.q: at this party, was having a Cafe Bulo party, at Tranchinas, which was at, Millenburg, at that, or Spanish Fort. We went out there, and played till about ten o'clock, that next day, it was one of the most rugged nights, we ever had in our lives. But we had some wonderful times, playing on that West…

249.t: Recording with Wooden Joe and Albert Burbank
249.s: Russell recalls a 1945-46 record with Wooden Joe; Francis recalls playing with Burbank and photos at Green Hall.
249.q: They got my picture, Albert Burbank, too. I played with him once. Albert Burbank's sheet. There was a bunch of us. They took our picture. Some of them down at the Green Hall. Because Albert told me he had my picture. Which hall was that? It's a Green Hall, way down Gentilly. I don't know that then.…

33.t: Records and Mr. Peer of OKeh
33.s: Asked about Russ Papalia on his records, he says nothing distinguished his records and begins a story about OKeh's Mr. Peer and a golf game.
33.q: But I would say here and now there is nothing of distinction attached to my records. I made a terrible mistake. A man came down here. No, I had a friend, Mr. Peer. He was a man that was doing his own piano house. And he was friendly with, no, I'm going to get the names all wrong. Mr. Peer was the…

848.s: He recalls only one recording session with Celestin, and cannot identify some titles.
848.q: I don't remember that. I don't remember either of these. I do remember the recording session that we had, but Sweetheart of TKO and Ta Ta Daddy, and we made others. Now, it may have been either of these two. It may have been both of them. I don't know.

260.t: Ray's first unreleased record in Richmond, Indiana
260.s: Ray's first record, made in Richmond, Indiana with Johnny Bayersdorffer's band shortly after the Wolverines recorded, was never released. Other recordings with the band are discussed.
260.q: Well, the first record I actually made never did come out. It was made in Richmond, Indiana, with Johnny Bisonoff, his band. Oh, yeah. But they never did release those records. It was just a little bit after the Wolverines made their records.

568.t: Records made with Richard M. Jones
568.s: Russell asks about recordings with Richard M. Jones; Hightower recalls using his own band, with Jones on piano.
568.q: And he used me and he used my clarinet player as Fred Palm and he used John Lindsay, my trombone player. Oh yeah. He's in y'all. He's in old now jazz. He played bass too. That's what you knew him is because in New Orleans he played bass when he's... Yeah. Thank you.

662.s: She made three or four records with Celestin, including My Josephine and Marrero's Station Calls, issued on Columbia 78s.
662.ch: Other pianists and the New Orleans scene
662.q: One was My Josephine. And other names that I just can't recall. John Marrera had several. And I was on those. That was when I first joined in 26, like I said.

186.t: Whether Willie's band ever recorded; Warner
186.s: He never recorded but might have; Warner played with him until he fell sick.
186.q: Never did. Never did. But I guess if he lived, he would have. Yeah, because he had good opportunity. If he lived, he'd have made records. It was a good band, I'm telling you. Warner and all of them can tell you. Y'all say you've been to Warner. Warner played with him a long time too. I don't know…

264.t: Records with George Lewis and Bunk Johnson
264.s: Zardis made records only with George Lewis and Bunk, at Canal Street and the Gypsy Tea Room.
264.q: Gypsy Tea Room, that's right. That's right. That's correct. That's right. That's correct. But you never get any of those records, I would have changed the name on them records, the label.

268.t: Recordings with Celestin and with Peter Bocage
268.s: Turner recorded with Celestin's band, filling in for Jeanette Kimball, and made a record with Peter Bocage.
268.ch: Early years and the Sonny South
268.q: Well, Mobile, there's no town, you know, if you had a town like that, you know. No, I made the first record with Peter on it. Not Peter on it, Peter Bocard. That's the only one I remember. But we broadcast from the states.

398.t: The railroad record with Wells and Robert Pete Williams
398.s: Maxey helped make a railroad work-song record with improvised tools, with Guitar Welch and Robert Pete Williams; talk about their whereabouts.
398.q: Well I didn't do it I seen the right smart of it did And of course I helped the boys Who put out a record of the railroad I hope them last year Put out a record of that Of course we well practiced it up Before we put it out And made a good hit out And made a good record out of it

461.t: The Victor recording Mr. African and Banjo Buck
461.s: Rene recorded for Victor in 1932 with Banjo Buck and trumpeter Claude Kennedy.
461.q: it was called Mr. African and who's that is a big band I remember they bought these guys got that stuff with Banjo Buck Banjo Buck

43.t: Later labels: Emerson, Melrose Stompers, Vocalion and Richard M. Jones
43.s: Allen runs through discography items. She recalls the 1939 Vocalion sides, Richard M. Jones as the connection to Melrose, and that she never recorded with Fletcher Henderson's band.
43.q: Yeah, but I wouldn't remember who the fellas were. Just like I tell you, you know, they just get any guy, you know, make up a combination like that, you see? So I wouldn't know who they were, who the fellas were. I wouldn't remember them, you know, who they were.

45.t: Records made in California c.1921 and Fred Washington
45.s: The interviewer says he made records in California around 1921 with Fred Washington; Williams recalls Washington playing at a nightclub in a makeshift band.
45.ch: Opening talk: pianists and Buddy Petit
45.q: Just like we making up nice. Yeah. He was just a make up band, like good fellas, you know.

776.t: Fate Marable's record, Dewey Jackson's Capitol Blues, and Crawford's record collecting
776.s: Crawford says Marable made one record and Jackson recorded Capitol Blues; Crawford describes his hobby.
776.q: You have to like it too with it, I guess.

878.s: Harry dates his first records to 1924-25 with Brownlee, tells of sharing composer credit on 'Peculiar' and 'Dirty Rag', and Russell reports on Brownlee in Pensacola.
878.q: See, Brown Lee, he was... That was his introduction to Peculiar Rank. Norman Brown Lee? Yeah. And of course, the other side was Sharky's tune. Let's see, what was the name of that? Dirty Rank. Oh, yeah. Yeah. So we decided that we'd use three names on both sides. But the verse and the chorus of…

924.t: The Paramount record and the So Different Four lineup
924.s: Allen and Jones go over the Paramount record of Homeward Bound Blues and Tiger Rag, its date and sidemen (Tapley, the Turners). Jones's nose whistle is played for the tape.
924.q: He lived here already. He was an original Louisville Jug Band. Mm-hmm. That, they're the names you don't can't remember the banjo. Mm-hmm.

634.t: Making records and playing for the governor
634.s: Happy remembers few recordings, played for the governor, and describes how hard studio work was.
634.q: We played for the governor. We played for the governor every Saturday, for 13 weeks. And yeah, last year, during Christmas time, some man come and went to the Deputy Institute and he bought one of those old records. What's that thing made? And the Deputy Institute people called me up and told me to…

1053.t: Earlier records with Nat Towles's orchestra
1053.s: He made records some years ago with Nat Towles but cannot recall the label or year.
1053.q: With, uh, Nat Toe's and his orchestra.

8.t: Nordskog, the singers and the Spikes brothers
8.s: Garland dealt only with the Spikes brothers; the two girls sang Spikes numbers; what became of the brothers; session timing.
8.q: Are they both living? No, John and the Spikes, uh, Rebs, Rebs living in the real estate business. Here in town. Do you ever see him? I've seen him quite a while. He's on Western Avenue. Western Avenue near, uh,

5.t: Other records: Johnny Dodds, Nat Dominique, O'Brien, Blythe, Ma Rainey
5.s: Asked about other recordings, he recalls Dodds on a Lil date, working with Dominique, and a date with Jimmy O'Brien that may have been Blythe's with Ma Rainey.
5.q: See, the Sunset, I think it was, I think it was with Carol, I believe. Might have been with him. Was it Cal? Yeah, I think it was Cal. Then, then he and I worked on dance jobs together too, Dominick. Remember making any records when Nanny was on the date? No, I, that, that's what I was just trying…

820.t: Owls recordings and the Jack Yates studio
820.s: Frank recalls recording in the Gacho building and Atlanta, and debates whether it was Jack Yates's studio.
820.q: I'm not going to hear... We made some recording. We made some up there in the Gacho building there. Or I think it was the Gacho building. Yeah. Gacho building. Yeah. Gacho building. That's where it was. Gacho building. And then we went to Atlanta to make that other trip. And I think that's... With…

54.s: McAllister never recorded, but Bud's band made records somewhere near Alexandria; he never learned if they were released.
54.ch: Bud's band: records, members, Douglas and Brundy
54.q: I think that we made some records and... What's the name of it? Uh... Through Fidelio over to... John... And... And... Through Fidelio over to... John... And... North from Johnville over to... Uh... Anything. I forget. Like you're going across the Red River, they're going into Bunky, coming from…

1043.t: Recording 'Ja-Da' and other records made in New York
1043.s: Christian recalls playing on a record of Ja-Da and a few others with a jazz band he hardly knew, being paid outright, and possibly Columbia records.
1043.q: No, I played it in the band. In the band I played it in. I played a couple of numbers that I played, but I can't remember the things.

56.t: Retakes and Dink Johnson on drums
56.s: Some sides came out first take; Dink Johnson stamped his feet so loudly a mattress was needed.
56.q: Oh, some of them came out... All right. Orish Kriotramon came out good first time. First time, right? But those... You know, the vocals, you know, wait to go with them again.

300.s: He recalls making a record but not the titles, and being asked to play again after construction work.
300.q: I have, uh, I have, uh, the fact I had one, I went to somebody around here, because I haven't got a clear. I've forgotten now who I learned it to. Yeah. A fellow and, uh, the doctor, you know, and Virginia gave me the record, you know, a small, a small album. Yeah. And, uh, did you rehearse for…

198.t: Playing with Buddy Petit; no early records
198.s: Barnes played often with Petit and Kelly but recalls no recordings before his late ones.
198.ch: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
198.q: Oh yeah, I played with Buddy, Austin. I mean a whole lot with Buddy. There wasn't no recording though. No, I don't remember no recording.

118.t: Recordings with Smiling Joe and Freddie Coleman
118.s: His few records, with Smiling Joe's band that worked at the Mardi Gras Lounge.
118.q: Records? Yeah. Did I make any records? Okay. Yeah, I did, uh, Kit Harvin. Uh, yeah. Nope. I didn't do too much recording. It's Freddie Coleman. Yeah, you made it. Yeah, I read some. Remember I already showed you that book? Yeah, Freddie Coleman, I did something with some people, I forgot, beat two,…

15.t: Other records: Roy Palmer, Biscuit Eater and Tiny Parham's last session
15.s: He cannot recall titles; he remembers Biscuit Eater and discovers years later that he played on Tiny Parham's Frogtown Blues.
15.ch: Chicago in the 1920s: Bix, Armstrong, Morton
15.q: I made quite a few with all of them. We went up into Richmond, Indiana. Jeanette. Yeah. And I made them with Roy Palmer. Don't ask me the names of them because I can't.

783.t: Records with Oliver and Jelly Roll Morton
783.s: Shoffner is unsure of the company for records with Morton, and says Oliver did not want his men recording with others.
783.q: and then see I made some records I guess the boys were making with Jilly Rue Morton well you made some of Jilly yeah now what them records was I don't know

58.t: Richard M. Jones and the Session company records
58.s: Punch recalls records with Jones before leaving Chicago.
58.ch: Records, Jimmy Wade and Richard M. Jones
58.q: Yeah, I made records with him. Richard M Jones, crippled fellow. Yeah, played piano. Where did you make the records with him? And John had none of them records? Man, I made plenty of records with Richard M Jones. No, I don't have any of the ones you made with him. Mr. Bill didn't have none? He…

707.t: First records: Irene Scruggs, Paramount and Vocalion
707.s: His first session was accompanying Irene Scruggs at Grafton, Wisconsin, then his own Paramount sides in 1929 and later Vocalion and Brunswick.
707.q: The very first records I made was with singer Irene Scruggs. They called it Chocolate Brown. She was out of St. Louis. She has a daughter over in Europe called Baby Scruggs. She's a showgirl now.

128.t: Robinson's record sessions after Sam Morgan
128.s: He lists records with Kid Rena, Kid Howard and Peter Bocage, and with Rudi Blesh, made in 1946.
128.q: Oh Rudy Blush ever came from town. Yeah, yeah, yeah, that's right. I'm sure of that. Rudy came, came, came, came here in 40, in 47 for, for a convo. Mm-hmm. Yeah, we made it, in 46, 46, yeah, Rudy came to the, yeah, but we, we, we, we was up there in 45, you know. And we came back, Rudy Blush came,…

352.t: Recording the James P. Johnson concert
352.s: Rayhill recorded James P. Johnson at the 1940s Hamilton concert; the tape went to the library and some tracks were later bootlegged on LP.
352.q: Yeah. In fact two of the records showed up on an LP, oh probably in the middle seventies. It showed one was bootlegged so it’s floating around.

740.t: Forgotten records: Al Casey, Jimmy Butler and the Fats Waller tribute
740.s: Overseas fans remind him of a trio record with Al Casey and Jimmy Butler, and a Fats Waller tribute with Slam Stewart, Johnny Guarnieri and Stephane Grappelli.
740.q: That’s who it was — I knew you could do it. Al Casey and Butler, Jimmy Butler. They were the two of them and the drum. Anyways he was Hugh Panassie’s son, who had this little, you know, recording company like. And he wanted to record different people so they said let’s put this together. So it was…

366.t: Fred Astaire's recording with Goodman: Who Cares
366.s: Sol urges Monk to find Astaire's record with Goodman's sextet.
366.ch: Current gigs and Goodman family stories
366.q: “Just Like Taking Candy From a Baby.” Great record. Great. Fred Astaire singing and dancing on both sides. And it’s so exciting, after he tap danced, the band came in. See he was tap dancing to the sextet. They gave him a stop time. Then the band came in like

1.t: Which New Orleans bands recorded locally
1.s: Barker and White list the few New Orleans bands that recorded, such as Sam Morgan, Celestin and Jones-Collins, while Piron recorded in New York.
1.q: No. None of them recorded. He didn’t record. Only one or two bands recorded here. That was Sam Morgan that came through, and somebody else. I think Sharkey [Bonano]. That’s all. Maybe Louis Dumaine.

368.t: Recordings and V-Discs with the Dorsey band
368.s: They discuss how many records he made with Dorsey and the V-Discs with the Dorsey trio.
368.q: I didn’t think so. Well, I know that we did a lot of those V-Discs. They used to, the ones for the Armed Services, they were calling them V-Discs. They were broadcasted and recorded, and we did many of those. A lot of those with just Dodo Marmaroso and Gene Krupa and myself, the trio in the Dorsey…

220.t: The Thad Jones tribute recording "One More"
220.s: Wess and Sara Tsutsumi try to recall who organized and played on the 2005 Thad Jones tribute recordings.
220.q: Maybe Jimmy Owens and Eddie Daniels. Yeah I remember that, that was nice. I never got a chance to play some of Thad’s music.

460.t: Victor Feldman's direct-to-disc Secret of the Andes
460.s: Laws recalls his first direct-to-disc recording, with Harvey Mason and others.
460.q: You record a whole side of a record direct-to-disc. So you can’t stop. So that was the very first. I think Harvey Mason was on that.

505.t: Recording with Indian musicians in Bombay on the State Department tour
505.s: On the India tour he and Beirach recorded Passing Dreams with four Indian musicians in a midnight TV studio, a highlight of his life.
505.q: Yes, on our trip to India, State Department tour, one of the highlights of my life. We organized, through some guy who knew Badal, to get four Indian musicians in the studio with us. Walked up four flights, dark, midnight. Got up there, little t.v. studio. There were 50 people sitting there like…

641.t: Recording four tunes for Okeh with Creath
641.s: Joe made four sides with Creath for Okeh but never heard them and would love a set.
641.ch: Southern Illinois roadhouse and St. Louis
641.q: No. And I haven't... I've met one who said that he heard them, and I said, 'Man, I'd give a million dollars for a set of them.' I can't think who it was. And he said... Maybe it was Zutty. He said, 'Maybe I'll try to get them. Maybe Marge can get them for you or something.' And that's the last I…

117.t: The album From Austin High Comes Jazz
117.s: Freeman recommends the 1938 New York Condon-group album with Tough and Teagarden that he fronted.
117.q: And when you think of that alone, or even if it had only been fifteen years, that is still a long time, still way ahead of his... And I think that when you suggested earlier that there isn't enough said about Dave, I certainly must agree with that, that I would like to suggest that fans go back to…
